virals.hook:
Iran Appears to Be Preparing a Convoy to Break Trump’s Blockade

This Saturday (21), tensions rose again in the Strait of Hormuz, with at least three oil tankers attacked, marking a new military escalation in the Persian Gulf.

This escalation comes as Iran prepares a large convoy of ships whose only goal can be breaking the naval blockade imposed by Trump.

Tehran is trying to take advantage of the window opened on Thursday (19), when Donald Trump stated, after meeting with Xi Jinping and Putin, that there is no urgency regarding Iran and that new strikes will only be discussed next year. Faced with an Iranian attempt to break the blockade, will Washington avoid a naval confrontation now so as not to sabotage its newly announced diplomatic pullback, or will it escalate too?

Over the past few days, more than 14 oil tankers at Kharg Island, the country’s main oil terminal, have been preparing to sail as a group toward the Gulf of Oman.

Unlike old vessels anchored without movement, satellite imagery and monitoring reports show that these 14 ships have taken on full crews, raised Iranian flags, and switched off their tracking transponders (AIS). These are operational navigation measures unnecessary for a ship that will merely sit anchored as storage.

Outlets linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), lawmakers, and Iranian religious leaders warned that if the U.S. fires a single bullet at the convoy, Iran will strike oil facilities in neighboring Persian Gulf countries, such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stated yesterday (20) that the blockade must be broken and that Tehran will make every effort to resume exports.

Even before the recent summit, Trump told Fox News that the U.S. does not need help from China or Russia to deal with Iran. This indicates that the Chinese and Russians have not yet agreed to increase pressure on Tehran to the levels Washington requested.

In practice, Beijing avoids pressuring Iran because a prolonged conflict in the Gulf keeps American forces tied down far from Asia, burning through ammunition and exposing vulnerabilities. 

Moscow, meanwhile, uses its partnership with the Iranians as a bargaining chip in negotiations over Ukraine, which, despite receiving positive gestures from Trump, have not yet reached terms favorable to Putin. The truth is that in this regard, Zelensky has been a good player and Putin is watching.

However, if Iran actually decides to move forward with a convoy of more than 14 tankers, what kind of escort would this group have against three aircraft carriers enforcing the blockade?

What is being planned is a three-layered escort:

Layer 1: Coastal fire with anti-ship missiles and artillery. Because the route from the Strait of Hormuz to the blockade zone passes just a few kilometers off the Iranian coast, mobile batteries hidden in tunnels and mountains, equipped with anti-ship cruise and ballistic missiles, cover this entire stretch and have the range to hit the carrier groups, even while they operate a few hundred kilometers offshore.

Layer 2: Surveillance drones and surface and underwater swarms. While reconnaissance drones such as the Mohajer and Ababil pinpoint the exact positions of U.S. warships to feed the land batteries, aerial suicide drones, unmanned explosive boats, and underwater vehicles (UUVs) operate to saturate U.S. Navy defenses and disrupt the blockade strategy.

Layer 3: Submarines and naval mines for area denial. Even with the heavy Kilo-class fleet reduced to just one submarine, several Ghadir-class coastal midget submarines remain active in shallow waters. They work as stealth platforms to lay smart mines, launch short-range missiles, and carry out torpedo ambushes against ships getting too close to the convoy’s route. I recall that some time ago, one of these submarines approached American warships and took photos without being detected.

virals.name: Drop Site
virals.hook:
🛢️ Iran will take "any action necessary" to break the US naval blockade, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Saturday, adding that Tehran has conveyed the warning to US and Qatari mediators, according to Iran's state news agency IRNA. Qatari officials held two hours of talks in Iran on Friday, he said.

The blockade has cut off Iran's seaborne crude exports since mid-July. Here's where things stand:

➤ More than 14 Iranian tankers are positioned at Kharg Island, with crews assigned and Iranian flags raised, as Iran prepares for a possible convoy toward the Gulf of Oman, Gulf News reported. Most have their transponders off.

➤ Vahid Ahmadi, a member of parliament's national security committee, claimed 14 tankers are already headed to their destinations, possibly under military escort, and that Iran has informed Qatar and Oman. "If we cannot sell oil, others should not be able to sell it either," he said.

➤ Tehran's own state media has sent mixed signals. Late Thursday, state broadcaster IRIB listed as "denied" reports that a tanker was being readied for export and that Iran would strike Gulf states' oil facilities if it were attacked. A Fars News Agency reporter had posted that threat on X, and Fars itself issued the denial. Tasnim separately denied that tankers were moving to break the blockade.

➤ No tanker or convoy has been confirmed to have made an attempt to break the blockade.

On Wednesday, US Central Command expanded the blockade to cover ship-to-ship transfers at sea. On Saturday, two tankers were hit in the Strait of Hormuz off Khasab, Oman, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency, and Iran said it shot down a US drone over Qeshm Island. The U.S. hasn’t confirmed.

University of Tehran professor Hassan Ahmadian said Iran is forcing a "binary" choice on Trump: let the tankers pass and his "blockade ends without an agreement or war," or attack them and face "Iranian responses that will be difficult for him to avoid." He appears to be suggesting Iran has already made its decision to test the blockade.

outsiders.name: Patricia Marins
outsiders.hook:
Iran Appears to Be Preparing a Convoy to Break Trump’s Blockade

This Saturday (21), tensions rose again in the Strait of Hormuz, with at least three oil tankers attacked, marking a new military escalation in the Persian Gulf.

This escalation comes as Iran prepares a large convoy of ships whose only goal can be breaking the naval blockade imposed by Trump.

Tehran is trying to take advantage of the window opened on Thursday (19), when Donald Trump stated, after meeting with Xi Jinping and Putin, that there is no urgency regarding Iran and that new strikes will only be discussed next year. Faced with an Iranian attempt to break the blockade, will Washington avoid a naval confrontation now so as not to sabotage its newly announced diplomatic pullback, or will it escalate too?

Over the past few days, more than 14 oil tankers at Kharg Island, the country’s main oil terminal, have been preparing to sail as a group toward the Gulf of Oman.

Unlike old vessels anchored without movement, satellite imagery and monitoring reports show that these 14 ships have taken on full crews, raised Iranian flags, and switched off their tracking transponders (AIS). These are operational navigation measures unnecessary for a ship that will merely sit anchored as storage.

Outlets linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), lawmakers, and Iranian religious leaders warned that if the U.S. fires a single bullet at the convoy, Iran will strike oil facilities in neighboring Persian Gulf countries, such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stated yesterday (20) that the blockade must be broken and that Tehran will make every effort to resume exports.

Even before the recent summit, Trump told Fox News that the U.S. does not need help from China or Russia to deal with Iran. This indicates that the Chinese and Russians have not yet agreed to increase pressure on Tehran to the levels Washington requested.

In practice, Beijing avoids pressuring Iran because a prolonged conflict in the Gulf keeps American forces tied down far from Asia, burning through ammunition and exposing vulnerabilities. 

Moscow, meanwhile, uses its partnership with the Iranians as a bargaining chip in negotiations over Ukraine, which, despite receiving positive gestures from Trump, have not yet reached terms favorable to Putin. The truth is that in this regard, Zelensky has been a good player and Putin is watching.

However, if Iran actually decides to move forward with a convoy of more than 14 tankers, what kind of escort would this group have against three aircraft carriers enforcing the blockade?

What is being planned is a three-layered escort:

Layer 1: Coastal fire with anti-ship missiles and artillery. Because the route from the Strait of Hormuz to the blockade zone passes just a few kilometers off the Iranian coast, mobile batteries hidden in tunnels and mountains, equipped with anti-ship cruise and ballistic missiles, cover this entire stretch and have the range to hit the carrier groups, even while they operate a few hundred kilometers offshore.

Layer 2: Surveillance drones and surface and underwater swarms. While reconnaissance drones such as the Mohajer and Ababil pinpoint the exact positions of U.S. warships to feed the land batteries, aerial suicide drones, unmanned explosive boats, and underwater vehicles (UUVs) operate to saturate U.S. Navy defenses and disrupt the blockade strategy.

Layer 3: Submarines and naval mines for area denial. Even with the heavy Kilo-class fleet reduced to just one submarine, several Ghadir-class coastal midget submarines remain active in shallow waters. They work as stealth platforms to lay smart mines, launch short-range missiles, and carry out torpedo ambushes against ships getting too close to the convoy’s route. I recall that some time ago, one of these submarines approached American warships and took photos without being detected.

outsiders.name: Drop Site
outsiders.hook:
🛢️ Iran will take "any action necessary" to break the US naval blockade, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Saturday, adding that Tehran has conveyed the warning to US and Qatari mediators, according to Iran's state news agency IRNA. Qatari officials held two hours of talks in Iran on Friday, he said.

The blockade has cut off Iran's seaborne crude exports since mid-July. Here's where things stand:

➤ More than 14 Iranian tankers are positioned at Kharg Island, with crews assigned and Iranian flags raised, as Iran prepares for a possible convoy toward the Gulf of Oman, Gulf News reported. Most have their transponders off.

➤ Vahid Ahmadi, a member of parliament's national security committee, claimed 14 tankers are already headed to their destinations, possibly under military escort, and that Iran has informed Qatar and Oman. "If we cannot sell oil, others should not be able to sell it either," he said.

➤ Tehran's own state media has sent mixed signals. Late Thursday, state broadcaster IRIB listed as "denied" reports that a tanker was being readied for export and that Iran would strike Gulf states' oil facilities if it were attacked. A Fars News Agency reporter had posted that threat on X, and Fars itself issued the denial. Tasnim separately denied that tankers were moving to break the blockade.

➤ No tanker or convoy has been confirmed to have made an attempt to break the blockade.

On Wednesday, US Central Command expanded the blockade to cover ship-to-ship transfers at sea. On Saturday, two tankers were hit in the Strait of Hormuz off Khasab, Oman, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency, and Iran said it shot down a US drone over Qeshm Island. The U.S. hasn’t confirmed.

University of Tehran professor Hassan Ahmadian said Iran is forcing a "binary" choice on Trump: let the tankers pass and his "blockade ends without an agreement or war," or attack them and face "Iranian responses that will be difficult for him to avoid." He appears to be suggesting Iran has already made its decision to test the blockade.
